fields.brief_block: A genuine issue of material fact exists when the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the non-moving party.
fields.opinion_block: summary judgment will not lie if the dispute about a material fact is “genuine,” that is, if the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion directly supports this proposition; the Court states summary judgment will not lie if the dispute over a material fact is genuine, meaning the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party. The brief's phrasing tracks the opinion nearly verbatim, and the pinpoint (page 248) aligns with the Court's discussion of the genuine-issue standard.

fields.brief_block: Summary judgment is a procedural tool designed to secure the "just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every action.
fields.opinion_block: Summary judgment procedure is properly regarded not as a disfavored procedural shortcut, but rather as an integral part of the Federal Rules as a whole, which are designed "to secure the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every action." Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 1
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion at page 327 directly supports this proposition, describing summary judgment as an integral part of the Federal Rules, which are designed "to secure the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every action" (quoting Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 1). The pinpoint and substance both match.

fields.brief_block: Mississippi courts have long held that a bill of exceptions statutory appeal is limited to challenges of a board's quasi-judicial or legislative actions, not its ministerial or administrative functions.
fields.finding_analysis: City of Madison v. Bryan is a zoning/building-permit case decided on grounds of standing, mootness, and the propriety of Rule 11 sanctions. It does not address any limitation on the scope of a bill of exceptions confining it to quasi-judicial or legislative actions as opposed to ministerial or administrative functions. The opinion does note in passing that "Each instance was clearly a separate legislative act by the City," but it never articulates or holds the distinction the brief attributes to it. The proposition finds no support in the cited text, and page 166 concerns Bryan's standing and mootness arguments, not the character of appealable municipal acts.

fields.brief_block: The City's reliance on Cutrera v. Board of Supervisors of Louisiana State University, 429 F.3d 108 (5th Cir. 2005), is inapposite. That case stands for the unremarkable proposition that a plaintiff cannot raise an entirely new cause of action at the summary judgment stage.
fields.opinion_block: A claim which is not raised in the complaint but, rather, is raised only in response to a motion for summary judgment is not properly before the court.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports the characterization. Cutrera held that the plaintiff's First Amendment retaliation claim under § 1983, which "was not raised in her complaint, and instead was raised for the first time in response to Appellee's motion for summary judgment," was "not properly before the court." That is precisely the proposition the brief attributes to the case.

fields.brief_block: (1) When determining whether to set aside default judgment, the Fifth Circuit directs courts to consider whether (1) the default was willful, (2) the non-defaulting party would be prejudiced, and (3) a meritorious defense has been presented. (2) willfulness turns on intentional failure to respond. (4) "mere delay does not alone constitute prejudice," but prejudice exists where delay results "in the loss of evidence, increased difficulties in discovery, or greater opportunities for fraud or collusion." (5) In short, it is not a "defense sufficient to support a finding on the merits for the defaulting party."
fields.opinion_block: Rather, “the plaintiff must show that the delay will result in the loss of evidence, increased difficulties in discovery, or greater opportunities for fraud and collusion.”
fields.finding_analysis: Each component tracks the opinion: it lists the three good-cause factors (willfulness, prejudice, meritorious defense), states that a finding of willful default rests on an "intentional failure of responsive pleadings," holds that "mere delay does not alone constitute prejudice" with the enumerated categories, and describes the meritorious-defense inquiry as whether the defendant presents a defense "sufficient to support a finding on the merits for the defaulting party." The only discrepancy is that the opinion says "fraud and collusion" while the brief quotes "fraud or collusion" — a trivial wording variance that does not alter the substance.

fields.brief_block: Courts in the Fifth Circuit routinely permit surreplies where a reply brief raises new issues to which the opposing party had no prior opportunity to respond.
fields.finding_analysis: Doe v. City of Memphis is a Sixth Circuit case about whether the district court abused its discretion under Rule 56(d) by granting summary judgment and striking class allegations before plaintiffs had a full opportunity to conduct discovery. It does not address surreplies, reply briefs raising new issues, or Fifth Circuit practice on responsive filings. The proposition finds no support anywhere in the opinion; the opinion concerns discovery diligence and the Plott factors, not briefing procedure.

fields.brief_block: Admissions obtained under Rule 36, including those deemed admitted through a party's failure to respond, can form the basis for summary judgment.
fields.opinion_block: Carls has plainly made Rule 36(a) admissions. These may be used for Rule 56 summary judgment.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion directly supports the proposition: it notes that Rule 36(a) issues "are deemed admitted unless a response or objection is filed within thirty days," that Carls failed to respond, and that such admissions "may be used for Rule 56 summary judgment." The quoted string is fabricated (not verbatim), but the substance is accurately supported.

fields.brief_block: (1) The admissions establish every element for judgment. (2) The Fifth Circuit recognizes that deemed admissions are judicial admissions that may not be contradicted and can alone support summary judgment. (3) Deemed admissions are "not mere evidence; they are conclusive judicial admissions" and are fully competent to support summary judgment.
fields.opinion_block: the court has the power to make exceptions to the Rule only when (1) the presentation of the merits will be aided and (2) no prejudice to the party obtaining the admission will result.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports the general point that Rule 36 admissions can support summary judgment and that Carls' admissions were sufficient ("It should be sufficient that Carls has admitted that it is an employer subject to FLSA and has failed to pay its pharmacists the overtime pay clearly due"). But the brief overstates by attributing to this Second Circuit opinion a Fifth Circuit doctrine that deemed admissions are "conclusive judicial admissions" that "may not be contradicted." The opinion actually emphasizes the district court's discretion under Rule 36(b) to permit withdrawal of admissions when the merits are served and no prejudice results, which cuts against any characterization of admissions as flatly uncontradictable. The distinctive quoted language does not appear in the opinion.

fields.brief_block: (1) The right to sue accrues at the moment of breach, not on the mere suspicion that a breach might occur. (2) Franconia Assocs. v. U.S. holds that a claim for repudiation of a contract accrues at the time the repudiation is treated as a breach.
fields.opinion_block: Such a repudiation ripens into a breach prior to the time'for performance only if the promisee "elects to treat it as such." ... "[t]he time of accrual... depends on whether the injured party chooses to treat the . . . repudiation as a present breach."
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports both propositions. It states that a breach claim accrues at the time of breach ("The cause of action for breach of contract accrues, and the statute of limitations begins to run, at the time of the breach"), and that a repudiation only ripens into a breach when the promisee elects to treat it as such, with accrual turning on that election. The pinpoint (page 143) corresponds to the repudiation/election discussion (Restatement §§235, 250; Roehm v. Horst).

fields.brief_block: It would be inconsistent with the purpose of the fee-shifting statute to dilute a fees award by refusing to compensate the attorney for the time reasonably spent in establishing and negotiating his rightful claim to the fee.
fields.opinion_block: The time spent so replying is compensable under § 1988. To hold otherwise would dilute the fee award and be inconsistent with the purposes of § 1988.
fields.finding_analysis: The proposition is substantively supported: the Cruz opinion holds that time spent establishing and litigating a fee claim is compensable and expressly states that refusing such compensation "would dilute the fee award and be inconsistent with the purposes of § 1988." That parallels the brief's proposition closely. However, the quoted string presented as a verbatim quotation does not appear in the opinion; the opinion's actual language differs (it does not use the phrasing "fee-shifting statute" or "establishing and negotiating his rightful claim"). The substance is sound, but the quotation is fabricated.

fields.brief_block: Defendant's failure to respond constitutes a waiver of any objections it might have asserted to Plaintiff's discovery requests.
fields.opinion_block: We readily agree with the district court that as a general rule, when a party fails to object timely to interrogatories, production requests, or other discovery efforts, objections thereto are waived.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion expressly states the general waiver rule the brief cites it for: untimely objections to discovery are waived. Note, however, that this case ultimately held the waiver rule did NOT apply to statutorily-privileged medical quality assurance records under 10 U.S.C. § 1102, so the case is an example of an exception to the rule even as it affirms the rule's general existence. For the general proposition asserted, the opinion's language directly supports it.

fields.brief_block: The Fifth Circuit has consistently upheld summary judgments based on deemed admissions.
fields.opinion_block: Moreover, this Court has affirmed a grant of summary judgment based on default admissions coupled with a district court's denial of a request to withdraw those admissions. See Dukes, 770 F.2d at 548.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports this general proposition: it holds that deemed admissions conclusively establish the matters admitted and can support summary judgment, and it expressly cites the Fifth Circuit's own precedent (Dukes) affirming summary judgment on default admissions, along with a string cite of similar cases in footnote 6. The pinpoint (420) is within the relevant discussion.

fields.brief_block: (1) The admissions establish every element for judgment. (2) The Fifth Circuit recognizes that deemed admissions are judicial admissions that may not be contradicted and can alone support summary judgment. (3) Deemed admissions are "not mere evidence; they are conclusive judicial admissions" and are fully competent to support summary judgment. (4) The Fifth Circuit has explained that prejudice involves real impairment in obtaining evidence, not merely having to prove a case. [...]
fields.opinion_block: Since Rule 36 admissions, whether express or by default, are conclusive as to the matters admitted, they cannot be overcome at the summary judgement stage by contradictory affidavit testimony or other evidence in the summary judgment record.
fields.finding_analysis: Propositions (1) and (2) are well supported: the opinion holds that the deemed admission conclusively established the validity of the tax deficiencies and that such admissions cannot be overcome by contradictory affidavit testimony and can support summary judgment. Proposition (3), however, presents a fabricated quotation -- the phrase "not mere evidence; they are conclusive judicial admissions" does not appear in the opinion, which instead speaks of matters being "conclusively established." Proposition (4) is not supported by this opinion: the court identifies prejudice as one of the two Rule 36(b) withdrawal factors but never defines prejudice as "real impairment in obtaining evidence, not merely having to prove a case"; that specific principle is absent. Proposition (5) is the brief's own argument, not a holding. Because the substantive core is supported but the quotation is fabricated and the prejudice principle is not in the opinion, the claim is partial.

fields.brief_block: Deemed admissions are "judicial admissions" that are binding on the party and cannot be contradicted at trial or on a motion for summary judgment.
fields.opinion_block: An admission that is not withdrawn or amended cannot be rebutted by contrary testimony or ignored by the district court simply because it finds the evidence presented by the party against whom the admission operates more credible.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports the proposition's substance: it holds that Rule 36 admissions are "conclusively established" and "cannot be rebutted by contrary testimony," and that this conclusive effect "applies equally to those admissions made affirmatively and those established by default." The precise phrase "judicial admissions" does not appear; the court instead describes a Rule 36 admission as "comparable to an admission in pleadings or a stipulation drafted by counsel for use at trial, rather than to an evidentiary admission," which is the same concept. The case arose post-trial rather than on summary judgment, so the summary-judgment gloss is a reasonable extension of the conclusive-effect holding rather than a direct statement, but the binding/non-contradictable core is squarely supported.

fields.brief_block: Rule 36 is self-executing: the City's failure to timely serve written answers results in conclusive judicial admissions. The Fifth Circuit recognizes that deemed admissions are judicial admissions that may not be contradicted and can alone support summary judgment. [...] Admissions are binding and cannot be contradicted to avoid summary judgment.
fields.opinion_block: Each matter on which an admission has been requested is admitted unless the party to whom the request is directed responds with a written answer or objection.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion directly supports the self-executing and conclusive nature of deemed admissions: a matter is admitted unless a timely written answer or objection is served, and "[t]his conclusive effect applies equally to those admissions made affirmatively and those established by default, even if the matters admitted relate to material facts that defeat a party's claim." It also holds admissions "cannot be rebutted by contrary testimony or ignored by the district court." The specific assertion that admissions "can alone support summary judgment" is not stated because this case reached the court post-trial, but that is a reasonable extension of the conclusive-effect holding rather than a contradiction; the binding, non-contradictable, self-executing core is squarely supported.

fields.brief_block: The court must view all evidence and draw all reasonable inferences in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.
fields.opinion_block: Respondents correctly note that "[o]n summary judgment the inferences to be drawn from the underlying facts . . . must be viewed in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion."
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion (around the cited page 587-588) directly endorses the proposition, quoting United States v. Diebold, Inc. for the rule that on summary judgment inferences from the underlying facts must be viewed in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion. Although Matsushita immediately qualifies this by noting that antitrust law limits the range of permissible inferences from ambiguous evidence, the general standard stated in the brief is accurately supported by the opinion.

fields.brief_block: Courts in the Fifth Circuit routinely permit surreplies where a reply brief raises new issues to which the opposing party had no prior opportunity to respond.
fields.finding_analysis: North Cypress Medical Center v. Cigna Healthcare is an ERISA case about a hospital's standing to sue an insurer for underpayment of benefits, ERISA preemption, RICO pleading, and statute of limitations for counterclaims. It does not address surreplies or briefing procedure. Page 203 of the opinion falls within the RICO analysis (§ 1962(c) distinctiveness); nothing in the opinion discusses when courts permit surreplies in response to new issues raised in a reply brief.

fields.brief_block: While the prevailing rate in the district where the court sits is a key factor, it is not the only one in determining how much to award in attorney's fees.
fields.opinion_block: To fulfill the purpose of Section 1988 fee awards, while accommodating Blum's and this court's focus on local forum rates for attorney fees, we hold that where, as here, abundant and uncontradicted evidence proved the necessity of Garrigan's turning to out-of-district counsel, the co-counsel's "home" rates should be considered as a starting point for calculating the lodestar amount.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports the proposition. While it reaffirms the Fifth Circuit's longstanding rule that local forum prevailing rates presumptively govern (a key factor), it holds that in unusual cases where out-of-district counsel are shown to be necessary, the co-counsel's home rates are the starting point, and the court retains discretion to adjust the lodestar and consider the twelve Johnson factors. This directly supports the notion that the local prevailing rate is important but not the sole determinant of an attorney's fee award. The pinpoint at page 381 corresponds to the section discussing prevailing community rates and the lodestar calculation.

fields.brief_block: The Fifth Circuit has consistently held that "the excusable neglect standard is a strict one" and that "inadvertence, ignorance of the rules, or mistakes construing the rules do not usually constitute excusable neglect."
fields.opinion_block: Where, as here, the rule at issue is unambiguous, a district court's determination that the neglect was inexcusable is virtually unassailable. Were it otherwise, "almost every appellant's lawyer would plead his own inability to understand the law when he fails to comply with a deadline."
fields.finding_analysis: The two quoted strings do not appear in the opinion (correctly flagged FABRICATED), so they cannot be presented as direct quotations. On substance, however, the opinion supports the underlying proposition: it holds that counsel's misreading of Rule 6(e) did not constitute excusable neglect, that "[t]he nature of this very mistake 'weighs heavily against a finding of excusable neglect,'" and that misinterpretations of unambiguous rules qualify only in "the rare case indeed." The strict-standard idea and the notion that mistakes construing the rules do not usually amount to excusable neglect are thus fairly grounded in the opinion, even though the specific quoted language is invented.

fields.brief_block: An attorney's customary billing rate is presumptively reasonable. 'An attorney's requested hourly rate is prima facie reasonable when he requests a rate that is within the range of rates he has charged paying clients for similar work in the recent past.'
fields.opinion_block: When an attorney's customary billing rate is the rate at which the attorney requests the lodestar be computed and that rate is within the range of prevailing market rates, the court should consider this rate when fixing the hourly rate to be allowed. When that rate is not contested, it is pri-ma facie reasonable.
fields.finding_analysis: Kellstrom directly supports the proposition that an attorney's customary billing rate is presumptively (prima facie) reasonable; the court, at the cited page 328 discussion, states that when a customary billing rate is within the range of prevailing market rates and uncontested, "it is prima facie reasonable," and cites Powell for the same holding. The brief's second sentence, however, is presented as a direct quotation but does not appear verbatim in Kellstrom's text (the opinion frames the rule in terms of "prevailing market rates" and the rate not being "contested," rather than "rates he has charged paying clients for similar work in the recent past"). Substantively the paraphrase is faithful to the opinion's holding, so the proposition is supported, though the quoted language is not the opinion's own.

fields.brief_block: The Supreme Court's caution against billing for purely secretarial tasks in Missouri v. Jenkins, 491 U.S. 274, 288 n.10 (1989), does not extend to essential professional activities, such as emailing or calling a client or reviewing and drafting legal documents.
fields.opinion_block: Of course, purely clerical or secretarial tasks should not be billed at a paralegal rate, regardless of who performs them. What the court in Johnson v. Georgia Highway Express, Inc. ... said in regard to the work of attorneys is applicable by analogy to paralegals: “It is appropriate to distinguish between legal work, in the strict sense, and investigation, clerical work, compilation of facts and statistics and other work which can often be accomplished by non-lawyers ... Such non-legal work may command a lesser rate.”
fields.finding_analysis: Footnote 10 (found at pages 288-289) accurately supports the proposition. It cautions that "purely clerical or secretarial tasks should not be billed at a paralegal rate," while distinguishing that caution from legal work, which retains its full compensatory value. The brief's point that this caution is limited to clerical/secretarial tasks and does not reach substantive professional legal activities is a faithful reading of the footnote; the specific examples the brief adds (emailing a client, drafting documents) are illustrations of the legal-work category the footnote leaves untouched.

fields.brief_block: Under Mississippi law, the question of when a plaintiff should have discovered an injury through the exercise of reasonable diligence is an issue of fact to be decided by a jury.
fields.opinion_block: [O]ccasionally the question of whether the suit is barred by the statute of limitations is a question of fact for the jury; however, as with other putative fact questions, the question may be taken away from the jury if reasonable minds could not differ as to the conclusion.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion supports the general idea that discovery-rule timing turns on factual questions of "what the plaintiff knew and when," and that this can be a jury question. However, the brief overstates the holding by presenting it as flatly an issue of fact for the jury. The opinion (quoting Smith) qualifies this: it is only "occasionally" a jury question, and the question "may be taken away from the jury if reasonable minds could not differ as to the conclusion." The brief omits this important qualification.

fields.brief_block: Wilkens involved unique circumstances not present here, including a pro se litigant and confusion regarding the application of the prison mailbox rule.
fields.opinion_block: Then as now, counsel of record for Wilkens was Mark W. Bred-ing, Esq., Tyler, Texas.
fields.finding_analysis: The brief characterizes Wilkens as involving a pro se litigant and confusion over the prison mailbox rule, but neither feature appears in the opinion. Wilkens was represented throughout by counsel of record (Mark W. Breding, Esq.), so it was not a pro se case. The opinion concerns whether a faxed copy of a judgment, received in hand by counsel, triggers the seven-day filing window under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(6)(A) for reopening the time to appeal; it never discusses or applies the prison mailbox rule. The cited unique circumstances are simply not present in this opinion.

fields.brief_block: Yilport reaffirmed the long-standing rule that a contract with a public board is formed only when entered on the minutes and that its terms cannot be varied by parol evidence.
fields.opinion_block: Such contracts when so entered upon the minutes may not be varied by parol nor altered by a court of equity[.]
fields.finding_analysis: The cited case is the opinion under review. It expressly reaffirms the minutes rule, stating that "public boards speak only through their minutes" and that "where a public board engages in business with another entity, no contract can be implied or presumed, it must be stated in express terms and recorded on the official minutes," and further that such contracts "may not be varied by parol nor altered by a court of equity." Both components of the proposition -- formation only via the minutes and non-variability by parol -- are directly supported.

fields.brief_block: Nor can a fee award substitute for Rule 55(c)'s threshold requirements; it is a discretionary condition available once "good cause" is established, not a device to manufacture it.
fields.opinion_block: Considering the lack of prejudice to plaintiff, along with the fact that the event of default ... was attributable to counsel ... and further considering that HamiltonDavis has presented meritorious defenses, the court concludes that the default judgment as to HamiltonDavis should be set aside. However, the court finds that plaintiff's reasonable attorney's fees and costs ... should be borne by defense counsel.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion illustrates the sequence the brief describes: the court first found "good cause" under Rule 55(c) (meritorious defense, lack of prejudice, default attributable to counsel) and only then imposed fees on defense counsel as a condition of setting the default judgment aside. To that extent the case supports the idea that a fee award follows once good cause is established. But the opinion never articulates the affirmative legal principle that a fee award "cannot substitute for" the threshold requirements or serve as "a device to manufacture" good cause; that framing is the brief's gloss, extending the case's practice into a rule it does not state.

fields.brief_block: Courts have consistently recognized that the purpose of the rules governing conflicts of interest is not only to protect the interests of clients but also to maintain the integrity of the judicial process.
fields.opinion_block: In short, the responsibility of an ethical lawyer, as an officer of the court and a key component of a system of justice, dedicated to a search for truth, is essentially the same whether the client announces an intention to bribe or threaten witnesses or jurors or to commit or procure perjury.
fields.finding_analysis: Nix v. Whiteside is an ineffective-assistance-of-counsel case about whether counsel's refusal to help present perjured testimony violates the Sixth Amendment; its central ethical theme is the attorney's duty of candor to the court and the trial as a "search for truth." The opinion repeatedly emphasizes that an attorney's duty to the client is limited by a duty to the legal system, which supports the general notion that ethics rules protect both clients and judicial integrity. However, the proposition is specifically framed around "rules governing conflicts of interest," and the opinion addresses conflicts of interest only to distinguish Cuyler v. Sullivan (noting the perjury "conflict" was of a "quite different kind"), not to explain the dual purpose of conflict-of-interest rules. The cited page (166) concerns cautioning courts against constitutionalizing professional-conduct standards, not the purpose of conflicts rules. The brief thus overstates by attributing a specific conflicts-of-interest principle to a case that grounds only the broader duty-to-the-judicial-system theme.

fields.brief_block: Scott v. Carpanzano is inopposite because there, the failure to answer reflected a single negligent omission.
fields.opinion_block: While their reliance on Mr. Carpanzano acting with the attorneys he retained may have been negligent, it does not amount to an ‘ ‘intentional failure’ to respond to litigation.’’
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion does support the general idea that certain defendants' failures to answer were negligent rather than willful: as to Ms. Belcastro and Ms. Carpanzano, the court found their reliance on Mr. Carpanzano "may have been negligent" but did not amount to an intentional failure to respond, and it reversed the district court's willful-default finding as to them. However, the opinion also found that Mr. Carpanzano willfully (intentionally) defaulted, so the case does not uniformly stand for a "single negligent omission." The brief's characterization as a "single negligent omission" simplifies and glosses the opinion's more nuanced, defendant-specific analysis, so the support is partial rather than complete.

fields.brief_block: The Fifth Circuit has consistently held that delays within a party's control do not constitute excusable neglect.
fields.opinion_block: There is no doubt that Silvercreek's counsel received the preliminary order through the esl website and should have noticed the blank space for the opt-out date. [...] counsel could have inquired of the court or other counsel as to the opt-out date. [...] The district court did not abuse its discretion in refusing to extend the opt-out date, because it considered Silvercreek's proffered evidence and determined that counsel's performance fell below the threshold required for neglect to be excusable.
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion does apply the Pioneer excusable-neglect standard and holds that Silvercreek's counsel's failure to identify and meet the opt-out deadline -- something within counsel's control, given access to the esl filings that mentioned the date -- was not excusable neglect. That reasonably supports the general idea the brief advances. However, the opinion does not articulate a broad, general rule that 'delays within a party's control do not constitute excusable neglect,' nor does it purport to describe a line of cases where the Fifth Circuit has 'consistently held' this. The court instead rests on the Halicki 'below-a-certain-threshold' framework and the abuse-of-discretion standard. The brief overstates a fact-specific holding into a sweeping consistent rule.

fields.brief_block: The statute of limitations for a breach of contract claim begins to run at the time of the breach.
fields.opinion_block: "[i]n the case of a breach of contract, the cause of action accrues at the time of the breach... ."
fields.finding_analysis: The opinion substantively supports the proposition: quoting Johnson v. Crisler, the Court states that "[i]n the case of a breach of contract, the cause of action accrues at the time of the breach," which is the basis for its holding that Young's limitations period did not begin running until Farm Bureau refused to pay. The brief's quoted sentence does not appear verbatim in the opinion (hence the fabricated-quote flag), but the principle it attributes to the case is accurately drawn from the opinion's text.
